newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends off in US, rally fizzles on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends off in US, rally fizzles on profit-taking.

text.p: The dollar closed weaker against the mark after profit-taking wiped out early gains on remarks by a senior German central bank official and a rally in stocks and bonds, experts said.
Traders also weighed the possibility of central bank intervention to boost the yen, a concern that kept the dollar from racking up any lasting gains against the Japanese unit.

Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer and Co in New York, described the dollar's retreat as "just an accumulation of profit-takers, nothing really out of the ordinary."
The dollar finished at 1.7275/80 marks, down from 1.7332/37 marks at the open. Against the yen, the dollar slid to 126.11/16 from 126.22/32.
The dollar had briefly surged to a fresh 37-month high of 1.7375 marks shortly after remarks by Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing.

On Tuesday, Issing said the launch of the single European currency, or euro, could cause shifts from investments denominated in marks into dollar-denominated investments. He said this applies particularly to the introductory phase, when the reputation of the euro will have to be established.
Issing spoke during a conference in Frankfurt, Germany on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), which is scheduled to began on January 1, 1999.

"I think it (the Issing remark) implies that we should see the dollar continue to be strong for some time until EMU either falls apart or gets solid enough for people to reinvest in those areas," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank.
Adding to the dollar's upward momentum was a rally in stock and bond markets following news that U.S. inflationary pressures were surprisingly tame in March.

The Labor Department reported that the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.1 percent overall in March and increased 0.2 percent excluding food and energy items. Economists polled by Reuters, on average, expected the March CPI to rise 0.2 percent overall and 0.3 percent in the core component.
The CPI report sent the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond up more than a full point and bolstered the Dow Industrial average, which scored a huge gain of 135 points on the day.
"The stock and bond markets both up today did not hurt at all," said Frank Pusateri, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Mellon Bank in Boston.

Although Pusateri hesitated to draw a direct correlation between the rise in the dollar and gains in stock and bond prices, he said: "But certainly from a psychological level, it certainly gave a lot of confidence to the move already under way."
That move higher, however, began to unravel by midday as some market participants sold dollars.
Throughout the session, the dollar failed to make much headway against the Japanese currency. Traders pointed to intervention fears as well as profit-taking.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka has vowed decisive action against excessive dollar/yen movements, but declined to specify a level that would trigger intervention.

Intervention is definitely on the minds of traders, but will probably not happen unless the dollar rises too fast towards 130 yen, said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York.

Elsewhere, the dollar ended at 1.4658/68 Swiss francs and Canadian $1.3965/70, down from 1.4720/30 francs and C$1.3979/84. Sterling rose to $1.6275/85 from $1.6273/83. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7725/30 from $0.7745/50.
